lessons.title: Understanding Idioms
lessons.concept: Idioms are expressions whose meanings are not directly deducible from the individual words. In verbal ability tests, you must recognize the figurative meaning. Learning common idioms and their standard meanings helps answer such questions accurately.
lessons.formula: Approach: recall or infer figurative meaning of the idiom -> match with the option that conveys the same idea.
lessons.worked_example: Idiom: 'Break the ice' — means to initiate conversation in a social setting to relieve tension or awkwardness, not literally breaking ice.
mistakes: Interpreting idioms literally from the words
Choosing an option that relates to only one word in the idiom
Confusing similar-sounding idioms with different meanings

lessons.title: Phrases and Their Usage
lessons.concept: Phrases in aptitude/verbal questions may test standard meanings or correct usage in context. Focus on the conventional meaning of the phrase as a whole and how it is typically used in sentences.
lessons.formula: Read the phrase as a unit -> identify its accepted meaning/usage -> select the option consistent with that meaning.
lessons.worked_example: Phrase: 'Once in a blue moon' means very rarely. Example: 'He visits his hometown once in a blue moon' implies infrequent visits.
mistakes: Ignoring frequency/intensity implied by the phrase
Picking an option that fits context loosely but not the phrase's meaning

lessons.title: Selecting Idioms/Phrases by Context
lessons.concept: Some questions give a situation or sentence and ask for the idiom/phrase that best fits. Understand the situation's key idea (e.g., difficulty, success, secrecy) and choose the expression that conveys that idea accurately.
lessons.formula: Identify situation key idea -> map to idiom meaning -> verify it fits tone and context.
lessons.worked_example: Situation: Someone revealed a secret unintentionally. The idiom 'let the cat out of the bag' fits because it means to disclose a secret.
mistakes: Choosing an idiom with related theme but wrong nuance
Not matching the idiom's tone to the situation
Relying on keyword overlap instead of meaning
